strengths: The paper addresses an important computational-imaging problem: using a single sparse-view CT reconstruction model across acquisition rates and image grids. Combining sinogram-domain spatial/frequency processing with physics-based unrolling is well motivated.

The reported reconstruction gains are substantial across two datasets. On the 10,000-slice kidney test set, CTO achieves 36.17/38.76/40.97 dB at 18/36/72 views, compared with 32.56/34.37/35.60 dB for the unrolled CNN. Patient-disjoint evaluation and additional full-test-set results strengthen the empirical evidence.
The reported 0.065-second inference time on an A100 is promising. Relative to the evaluated 1,000-step diffusion implementations, Table 2 supports the claimed greater-than-500-fold speed advantage.

The manuscript attributes its DISCO and UDNO components to prior work and provides useful design ablations: detector-axis frequency processing performs best among the tested Fourier configurations, and flipped circular padding improves reconstruction PSNR by 0.83 dB.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is only partially established. Section 5.2 trains jointly on all four evaluated sampling rates, demonstrating multi-rate fitting rather than generalization to unseen rates. The separate 72-to-144-view experiment is relevant, but lacks a quantitative test-set table, uncertainty, and comparison with a model trained at the target rate. Broader held-out-rate evaluation is needed to support the claimed acquisition flexibility.

The image-resolution experiment does not establish recovery of genuinely higher-resolution anatomy. Section 5.3 evaluates against bilinearly interpolated ground truth and also upsamples the intermediate reconstruction. This tests behavior on a denser grid, but cannot demonstrate recovery of additional spatial information. The reported advantage over a directly transferred CNN also lacks a simple control that reconstructs at the training resolution and then interpolates. Native-resolution targets and aggregate results would materially strengthen this central contribution.

The claim that the complete CTO architecture is inherently rotation-equivariant is not justified. The image-space DISCO kernels explicitly contain learned anisotropic basis functions; ordinary Cartesian convolution with such kernels does not generally commute with rotations. Appendix A addresses angular translation of a sinogram convolution, but does not establish equivariance of the complete encoder–decoder, image-space updates, or their composition. Flipped padding alone is insufficient. The qualitative rotations and padding ablation demonstrate useful robustness, not the asserted architectural guarantee.

The main CNN comparison does not isolate neural operators as claimed. Section 5.2 describes replacing DISCO with regular convolutions, whereas Appendix B.2 states that the CNN baseline omits learned sinogram processing entirely. Thus the gain also includes additional dual-domain processing. A matched dual-domain CNN, along with an image-only DISCO ablation, is needed to establish how much improvement comes from continuous kernels versus the overall architecture. This matters because DISCO, UDNO, and operator-based reconstruction are inherited from prior work.

Baseline validity and training adequacy require clarification. The diffusion prior is trained for only 2,000 iterations, without convergence evidence, making broad superiority claims over state-of-the-art diffusion methods premature. SART uses only five sweeps, and its reported kidney performance barely improves as views increase. Moreover, the stated scikit-image iradon_sart implementation assumes parallel-beam geometry, whereas AAPM experiments use fan-beam data; no rebinning or geometry adaptation is described. These concerns do not negate the learned-baseline gains, but weaken the breadth of the comparative claims.

Reproducibility and deployment evidence remain incomplete. The manuscript omits CTO's training duration, important projector and normalization details, and how data-consistency scaling and quadrature change with resolution. Experiments use simulated projections without a specified measurement-noise protocol or demonstrated robustness to realistic acquisition noise. Consequently, the clinical-deployment language exceeds the present evidence. Overall, the promising reconstruction results do not yet resolve the shortcomings in the paper's principal generalization and equivariance claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision inverse problem: reconstructing sparse-view CT with a single model across acquisition rates and image grids. Combining sinogram-domain spatial/frequency processing with image-domain unrolling is technically motivated, and the underlying DISCO and UDNO methods are appropriately attributed.

The reported reconstruction improvements are substantial across two datasets with patient-separated train/test splits. On the full kidney test set, CTO achieves 36.17/38.76/40.97 dB at 18/36/72 views, compared with 32.56/34.37/35.60 dB for the unrolled CNN. The supplementary results extend evaluation beyond the 500-slice subset used for diffusion comparisons.
The measured 0.065-second inference time is promising. Frequency-processing and boundary-padding ablations provide useful evidence that these design choices improve reconstruction accuracy.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is insufficiently demonstrated. Section 5.2 trains jointly on the same 9/18/36/72-view settings used for evaluation; these results establish multi-rate fitting, not generalization to unseen rates. Section 5.3 adds a 72-to-144-view experiment, but provides only example images and a stated gain, without a dataset-level table, uncertainty, or clear evaluation sample size. Broader held-out-rate and angular-offset tests are needed to substantiate the claimed sampling independence.

The image-resolution experiment has a limited target: both the intermediate reconstruction and ground truth are bilinearly enlarged from 256×256 to 512×512. This can test behavior under grid refinement, but does not establish recovery of native high-resolution detail. It also lacks an essential control: reconstructing at the training resolution and then interpolating the final output. Consequently, the experiment does not convincingly establish the claimed zero-shot super-resolution advantage.

The claimed inherent rotation equivariance of the complete CTO architecture is not established. Appendix A discusses angular-shift equivariance of a sinogram convolution, whereas the image-space operator uses Cartesian DISCO kernels with anisotropic bases; these are not automatically rotation-equivariant. The argument also does not establish equivariance through the multiscale pooling operations. Figure 3's qualitative rotations and Table 5's 0.83 dB padding improvement demonstrate neither exact equivariance nor a measured equivariance error. This is a substantive issue because equivariance is an explicit principal contribution.

The CNN comparison does not isolate the contribution of function-space kernels. Although the main text describes the baseline as replacing DISCO with ordinary convolutions, Supplementary B.2 states that the CNN operates entirely in image space and has no learned sinogram processing. CTO therefore changes both the convolution parameterization and the processing architecture. A matched dual-domain spatial/frequency CNN, together with separate image-only and sinogram-only operator ablations, is needed to attribute the gains. This matters particularly because DISCO, UDNO, and neural-operator unrolling already build closely on cited prior work.

Several baseline choices weaken the broad superiority claims. The 65-million-parameter diffusion prior is trained for only 2,000 iterations, without convergence evidence, while the speed comparison uses 1,000-step sampling without a quality–latency sweep. SART receives only five iterations. Furthermore, the stated scikit-image iradon_sart implementation assumes parallel-beam geometry, whereas AAPM measurements are described as fan-beam; no rebinning or compatible adaptation is documented. These concerns do not negate the reported learned-baseline gains, but limit conclusions about competitive reconstruction methods generally.

Reproducibility and deployment evidence remain incomplete. The manuscript omits CTO's training duration, important physical-coordinate/quadrature normalization details across resolutions, and how complex Fourier features are handled. The measurements are synthetically generated, with no specified experimental noise model or evaluation on measured projections. Separate parallel-beam and fan-beam dataset experiments also do not demonstrate transfer of one trained model across geometries. These limitations materially narrow the claims of acquisition robustness and practical clinical applicability.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computational imaging problem: reconstructing sparse-view CT with one model across acquisition rates and image resolutions. Combining continuous-kernel operators with physics-based unrolling is well motivated.

Reported reconstruction gains are substantial and consistent across two datasets with patient-disjoint splits. On the kidney subset, CTO achieves 36.11/38.68/40.83 dB at 18/36/72 views, outperforming the evaluated learned baselines. The larger 10,000-slice evaluation supports these improvements.

The sinogram module incorporates useful CT-specific structure through spatial and detector-frequency processing and physically motivated angular padding. Frequency-branch and padding ablations provide evidence that these choices improve reconstruction quality.
The reported 0.065-second inference time on an A100 demonstrates practical potential. Relative to the evaluated 1,000-step diffusion implementations, the claimed speed advantage is supported.

The presentation explains the architecture and physical motivation clearly, and appropriately credits prior DISCO, UDNO, and unrolled reconstruction methods. The contribution is principally their CT-specific adaptation and integration.
weaknesses: The claim that the complete CTO architecture is inherently rotation-equivariant is not established. Appendix A addresses an angular convolution, whereas the image-space operator uses Cartesian DISCO kernels with learned anisotropic components; such kernels are not automatically rotation-equivariant. Encoder–decoder downsampling also requires consideration. Figure 3's rotated examples and Table 5's 0.83 dB padding improvement demonstrate useful behavior, but do not measure equivariance error or establish the stated architectural guarantee.

Evidence for the central resolution-generalization claim is limited. Section 5.3 evaluates 512×512 outputs against bilinearly interpolated ground truth, which tests behavior on a finer grid rather than recovery of native high-resolution detail. It lacks a reconstruct-at-training-resolution-then-upsample control and comprehensive quantitative results across resolutions. Moreover, the main multi-rate experiments train jointly on the evaluated rates; they establish shared-model performance, not unseen-rate generalization. The separate 72-to-144-view experiment is encouraging but insufficiently characterized.

The main CNN comparison does not isolate the benefit of continuous kernels. Section 5.2 describes the baseline as replacing DISCO with regular convolutions, but Appendix B.2 states that it omits learned sinogram processing entirely. Consequently, the reported approximately 4 dB gain conflates operator design with the addition of a dual-domain, spatial–frequency module. A CNN counterpart with the same branches and reconstruction pipeline is needed.

Baseline validation leaves important uncertainty. The 65-million-parameter diffusion prior is trained for only 2,000 iterations, without convergence evidence or a quality-versus-runtime comparison. FBP's approximately 7 dB kidney results warrant checking normalization and projector consistency. Appendix B also specifies scikit-image's parallel-beam iradon_sart implementation while describing fan-beam AAPM measurements, without explaining any required rebinning. These concerns do not negate all learned-baseline gains, but weaken broad superiority claims.

Reproducibility and deployment evidence need strengthening. The manuscript omits CTO's training duration and important details of quadrature normalization, complex-valued frequency processing, and cross-resolution data-consistency implementation. The flipped angular boundary construction is justified for parallel-beam data, but its adaptation to the fan-beam experiment is unclear. Evaluation uses generated sinograms without a specified measurement-noise protocol, limiting conclusions about real acquisition robustness.

Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the promising empirical improvements do not yet resolve the unsupported equivariance claim and the experimental gaps surrounding resolution independence and causal attribution. These are central to the scientific case rather than presentation-only corrections.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computational imaging problem: using one CT reconstruction model across acquisition rates and image discretizations. The combination of continuous DISCO kernels, dual-domain processing, and physics-based unrolling is well motivated.

Reported reconstruction improvements are substantial. On AAPM, CTO achieves 31.57/35.06/37.88 dB at 18/36/72 views, versus 29.14/31.76/33.35 dB for the unrolled CNN. Supplementary results extend the evidence to held-out kidney patients and lung CT.

The experimental coverage includes component ablations, single-rate training, noise robustness, cross-dataset transfer, and computational cost. Table 11 reports a 1.97 dB improvement for a parameter- and FLOP-matched variant, providing useful evidence beyond simply increasing model capacity.
The reported 65 ms inference time is practically attractive. The manuscript generally explains the architectural motivation clearly and attributes the underlying DISCO, UDNO, and unrolling methods.
weaknesses: The principal CNN comparison is internally inconsistent, undermining attribution of the gains to neural operators. Section 5.1 describes an identical architecture with DISCO replaced by conventional convolutions, whereas Supplement B.2 explicitly says the CNN operates entirely in image space without learned sinogram processing. Consequently, the comparison may conflate continuous kernels with adding the entire spatial–frequency sinogram module. Table 11's parameter/FLOP matching does not resolve this architectural ambiguity. A fully matched dual-domain CNN control is essential.

The claimed rotation equivariance of the complete reconstruction network is not established. Appendix A only analyzes stationary sinogram convolution; the image-space operator uses unconstrained anisotropic Cartesian kernels, which are not generally rotation-equivariant, and the U-shaped pooling operations introduce additional shift-equivariance issues. Even the sinogram argument does not establish that arbitrary kernels preserve the identification f(θ+π,r)=f(θ,−r), which requires compatibility with detector reflection. The padding ablation and qualitative rotations demonstrate useful robustness, but not the stated architectural guarantee.

The zero-shot image super-resolution experiment does not demonstrate recovery of higher-resolution anatomy: both the intermediate reconstruction and ground truth are bilinearly upsampled to 512×512. This supports evaluation on a finer grid, but not the stronger claims about recovering fine detail. Native high-resolution targets and a baseline that reconstructs at the training resolution and then upsamples are needed. For sinogram-resolution transfer, Section 5.3 reports relative improvements without a complete table of absolute performance; the illustrated CTO results are only approximately 15–16.5 dB.

Most headline multi-rate results evaluate the same rates used during training, establishing joint multi-rate performance rather than broad unseen-rate generalization. The 72-to-144-view experiment provides some extrapolation evidence, but does not establish consistent behavior across unseen sparsity levels or discretizations. Discretization convergence of a kernel approximation also does not itself guarantee reconstruction accuracy under changing measurement information. These distinctions matter because generalization is the central contribution.

Baseline adequacy remains uncertain. The diffusion prior is trained for only 2,000 iterations, without convergence evidence or a matched training-budget analysis, yet its results support broad superiority claims over diffusion methods. The closely relevant multi-rate method MVMS-RCN [19] is discussed but not evaluated. Supplement B.2 also specifies scikit-image iradon_sart, a parallel-beam method, while AAPM uses fan-beam measurements; any necessary rebinning or geometry adaptation is unexplained. These issues require clarification before accepting the comparative claims.

Important implementation details remain unresolved: the abstract's code link is blank, CTO's training duration is unspecified, and complex-valued frequency processing and discretization-dependent quadrature/forward-operator normalization are insufficiently described. The parallel-beam flipped-padding and Fourier-slice arguments are also not reconciled with the fan-beam AAPM implementation. Overall, the promising empirical results support further investigation, but the architectural comparison and central theoretical claims require substantive correction and validation.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computational imaging problem: reconstructing CT images with one model across acquisition rates and image discretizations. Integrating continuous-kernel operators into a physics-informed, dual-domain reconstruction pipeline is a plausible contribution under Algorithms/General.

Reported reconstruction gains are substantial. On AAPM, CTO achieves 31.57/35.06/37.88 dB at 18/36/72 views, compared with 29.14/31.76/33.35 dB for the unrolled CNN. The supplement extends evaluation to 10,000 held-out kidney slices and a lung dataset, and includes single-rate comparisons.

The spatial–frequency sinogram design has a sensible connection to the Fourier slice theorem. Branch ablations and the detector-axis FFT comparison provide evidence that these components improve reconstruction.

The reported 0.065-second inference time is practically attractive. Patient-separated splits for the principal datasets, noise and cross-dataset experiments, and the parameter-matched result in Table 11 are useful evaluation efforts.
weaknesses: The central CNN comparison is inconsistently specified. Section 5.1 describes the same architecture with DISCO replaced by ordinary convolutions, but Supplement B.2 explicitly says the CNN operates entirely in image space without learned sinogram processing. Consequently, the headline gains may combine continuous parameterization with additional dual-domain processing. Table 11 reports a matched-architecture variant with a promising 1.97 dB gain, but does not explain its modules sufficiently to resolve this contradiction or evaluate it across rates and resolutions. A clearly specified, dual-domain CNN control is needed to establish the claimed source of improvement.

The claimed rotation equivariance of the complete CTO is not established. Supplement A discusses a stationary sinogram convolution; it does not establish equivariance of the Cartesian image operator with learned anisotropic kernels or of the encoder–decoder's downsampling operations. Furthermore, flipped padding alone does not establish that arbitrary kernels preserve the sinogram's pi-periodicity-with-detector-flip constraint. The 0.83 dB padding ablation demonstrates a useful boundary treatment, but reconstruction PSNR and a few rotated examples do not measure equivariance error. The architecture needs additional justification or the claim should be narrowed to rotational robustness.

The acquisition geometry introduces an unresolved technical inconsistency. Supplement B.1 uses fan-beam AAPM data over [0, 2pi), whereas the derivation and flipped-boundary construction concern parallel-beam data over [0, pi). The manuscript does not explain geometry-specific padding or rebinning. It also specifies scikit-image iradon_sart, a parallel-beam reconstruction routine, without explaining how it handles the fan-beam experiment. These omissions affect both the physical argument and confidence in the baseline comparison.

Evidence for resolution generalization is weaker than the super-resolution claims imply. Section 5.3 evaluates 512-by-512 outputs against bilinearly enlarged 256-by-256 ground truth, so it tests operation on a finer grid rather than recovery of additional anatomical detail. An upsampled native-resolution reconstruction is an essential missing control. The main multi-rate tables evaluate rates included in training; the unseen 144-view experiments are useful, but report relative gains without comprehensive absolute results or a broader held-out-rate evaluation.

Baseline validation is insufficient for the broad state-of-the-art claims. The diffusion prior is trained for only 2,000 iterations, with no convergence evidence or training-budget sensitivity. The very low FBP results, including approximately 7.5 dB at 72 views on the full kidney test set, merit checks of scaling and reconstruction geometry. The directly relevant multi-rate method MVMS-RCN [19] is discussed but not evaluated. These concerns do not negate the reported gains, but weaken their interpretation.

Reproducibility and robustness reporting remain incomplete. The supplied abstract has an empty code link, CTO's training duration is unspecified, and implementation details for complex-valued frequency features and discretization-dependent normalization are missing. Supplement C.5 gives only average improvements for noise and cross-dataset transfer, without absolute performance or enough detail to interpret the accompanying geometry change. Overall, the promising empirical results do not yet resolve the methodological and evidential concerns surrounding the paper's central claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reconstructing CT images with one model across acquisition rates and output resolutions. The combination of continuous DISCO kernels, spatial–frequency sinogram processing, and physics-based unrolling is well motivated.

Reported multi-rate improvements are substantial. On AAPM, CTO achieves 31.57/35.06/37.88 dB at 18/36/72 views, versus 29.14/31.76/33.35 dB for the unrolled CNN. Kidney and supplementary lung results provide additional evidence of usefulness across anatomies.

The experimental coverage includes component ablations, single-rate training, cross-dataset transfer, noisy measurements, and computational costs. Supplementary Table 8 usefully shows that CTO also improves over selected baselines under their conventional single-rate protocol.

The reported 0.065-second inference time and moderate parameter count make the approach potentially practical. Existing DISCO and UDNO components are attributed, and the architectural presentation is generally understandable.
weaknesses: The central CNN comparison is inconsistently specified. Section 5.1 describes the baseline as the same architecture with DISCO replaced by conventional convolutions, whereas Supplement B.2 explicitly says it operates entirely in image space without learned sinogram processing. These are materially different controls. If the latter description is correct, the gains conflate continuous kernels with additional dual-domain processing. Supplementary Table 11 matches parameter counts and FLOPs but does not resolve this architectural ambiguity.

The claimed rotation equivariance of the complete CTO is not established. Supplement A discusses a stationary sinogram convolution, but the image-space network uses anisotropic Cartesian kernels without rotational constraints, and the U-shaped architecture includes pooling that requires separate equivariance analysis. Furthermore, flipped padding alone does not establish that arbitrary learned kernels preserve the required detector-reflection identification. The padding ablation and examples at 0, 90, and 180 degrees support rotational robustness, rather than the stronger end-to-end SO(2)-equivariance claim.

The acquisition geometry and mathematical justification are insufficiently reconciled. The Fourier-slice argument and pi-periodicity-with-detector-flip construction assume parallel-beam measurements, whereas Supplement B.1 uses fan-beam geometry over a full rotation for AAPM. The manuscript does not explain the corresponding changes to padding or frequency processing. It also specifies scikit-image iradon_sart, a parallel-beam reconstruction routine, without explaining how the fan-beam baseline is handled.

Evidence for resolution generalization is narrower than the claims suggest. Section 5.3 evaluates image super-resolution against bilinearly upsampled ground truth, which tests transfer between grids but cannot demonstrate recovery of genuine higher-resolution anatomy. Most multi-rate results evaluate rates included in training. The unseen 144-view experiments are useful, but broader quantitative testing across unseen resolutions and sampling rates, including simple resize-based CNN controls, is needed to substantiate the general resolution-agnostic claim.

Some headline comparisons need stronger validation. The 65-million-parameter diffusion prior is trained for only 2,000 iterations, with no convergence evidence, while inference uses 1,000 steps. Consequently, the reported fidelity and 500-fold speed advantages are specific to this setup and do not establish a general advantage over competitive diffusion reconstruction. The manuscript also acknowledges an existing multi-rate method by Fan et al. but does not compare against it.

The evidence isolating the neural-operator design remains incomplete. There is no reconstruction-accuracy comparison with alternative neural operators; Supplement D substitutes complexity estimates and an unsupported assertion that global FNO mixing necessarily oversmooths images. Reproducibility is also limited by the missing code link, unspecified CTO training duration, and incomplete lung-data split details. Together with the architectural and equivariance issues above, these concerns prevent a convincing acceptance case despite the promising empirical results.
